name: Charcoal
lede: Charcoal is the dark grey of burnt wood, the oldest drawing black there is, from the bison of Altamira to the willow sticks in a modern art room.

sections.title: The swatch and the stick
sections.body:
Charcoal is what is left when wood is heated until it turns to black carbon. As a color word it has meant two slightly different things: the black of the drawing stick, and a dark grey [1]. Paterson's dictionary lists charcoal as a dark grey, charcoal brown as a dark brown, and charcoal grey as another dark grey, and it adds that charcoal black is an ancient pigment also called carbon black [1].

The swatch here, #36454F, is a cool, slate-leaning dark grey [15]. It is a screen idea of burnt wood, not a measurement of it. Coles notes that the ancient Egyptians preferred lamp black to the grey-black of charcoal, which is a useful reminder that real charcoal is greyer than true black [5]. Its nearest named neighbor in our data is [[charcoal-grey]], 5.7 units away, with [[slate-grey]] and [[gunmetal]] in the same dark-grey family and [[black]] one step beyond [15].

sections.title: The first black
sections.body:
Charcoal is among the oldest pigments there is. Ball lists the cave painters' palette as red and yellow earths from iron oxide, green earths, brown from manganese oxide, white from chalk and bone, and black from charcoal [4]. Gurney, writing for painters, agrees that blacks, reds and yellows were the easy colors to find, which is why they appear in the earliest art [11].

Finlay tells the story of Altamira in northern Spain, found in 1879 when the amateur archaeologist de Sautuola's young daughter looked up and saw bison on the ceiling [3]. The charcoal there is applied in wide, confident sweeps that double as outline and shadow, with red and yellow ochre painted over them [3]. In Finlay's reckoning the images had not been seen by human eyes for about 15,000 years [3]. The Chauvet cave in the Ardeche, found in 1994, holds paintings at least twice as old, and its Panel of the Horses is one of the most striking uses of charcoal in prehistoric art [3]. Finlay dates Chauvet at about 30,000 years, and notes that all these caves were painted with charcoal and ochres, with rare exceptions such as the Magura caves in Bulgaria, apparently painted brown with bat guano [3].

Radiocarbon dating makes charcoal doubly useful, since the same carbon that painted the line can be tested for its age, and the compendium cites several measurements on rock-art sites [2].

sections.title: A girl, a shadow and a legend
sections.body:
Pliny told a tale of the origin of painting, which Finlay retells [3]. A young woman of Corinth, saying goodbye to her lover, saw his shadow on the wall by candlelight, reached into the fire for a piece of charcoal, and traced the outline [3]. Finlay calls it a mythic image, and the legend became a favorite with Georgian and Victorian artists, including David Allan, whose 1775 painting *The Origin of Painting* shows the scene [3]. The point of the story is still true to the material: a burnt stick from any fire will draw, and a drawn line is the first step of most paintings [3].

The tale also fits the way painters really start. Finlay watched an icon painter transfer a pencil sketch to a gessoed panel, and artists in Indonesia sketch in charcoal before adding paint to Hindu story designs [3]. Pastoureau notes the same order for the Impressionists, who prepared the canvas, sketched in pencil or charcoal, and then laid in the paint [13].

sections.title: Willow, vines and the baker's oven
sections.body:
The best drawing charcoal is made from willow. Cennino Cennini, in the fourteenth century, recommended willow for drawing, saying no coals anywhere were better [3]. He told readers to bundle the sticks, seal them in a new casserole, and leave it overnight in the baker's oven after the baker had finished work [3]. Ball adds that medieval English painters, who were tradesmen like any other, would ask the baker for the use of his ovens to make charcoal for black pigment [4].

The craft has a modern origin story too. In the mid-1950s Percy Coate, a Somerset willow grower whose basket trade was failing, hurt his back and lay by the fire, where he spotted a perfect piece of burnt willow that had rolled out of the ashes [3]. He began roasting willow in biscuit tins, and the business became PH Coate, which Finlay calls Britain's main supplier [3]. In a note, Finlay reports 85 acres of willow producing about 1.5 million stems yearly, half of them burned for charcoal [3].

Other woods give other blacks. Coles says that vine charcoal, made from dried grapevines, gives the deepest blue-black there is, and that the most prized charcoal is made from vines [5]. Church, in 1901, wrote that coconut yields the densest, most velvety black, vine shoots a less solid, bluish black, and washed wine lees a rich black, which was sold as Frankfort black [2].

sections.title: Charcoal as paint
sections.body:
Charcoal is also a pigment, not only a crayon. The Pigment Compendium lists analyses that found it in Roman wall paintings at Pompeii and other sites, on Canosa vases in the Getty, at the first-century Moche site of La Mina, and on a Norwegian carved lion of the twelfth or thirteenth century [2]. It was found in medieval playing cards of about 1430, in English wall paintings, and, among named painters, in work by Rembrandt, Vermeer, Jan Steen and Constable, and in van Gogh's paintings from Arles in 1888 and 1889 [2].

The Spanish painter Francisco Pacheco wrote in 1638 that the usual shadow color was charcoal black [2]. Gage reports, from the English traveller Richard Symonds, that the Italian painter Giovanni Angelo Canini set his palette about 1630 in two rows, one of unmixed pigments running from white and yellow ochre to charcoal black [7]. As a drawing material, Gage reports that Leonardo's large cartoon of the Madonna and Child with St Anne uses charcoal with white chalk, and the compendium notes charcoal in cartoons by Annibale and Agostino Carracci for the Palazzo Farnese in Rome [7][2].

In the nineteenth century charcoal reached the paint box under a color name. The British colormen Winsor and Newton and Reeves sold a charcoal grey in the 1890s, made from charcoal [2].

sections.title: Blue black, vine black and ivory
sections.body:
Charcoal blacks are not all the same, and the old names kept track. The compendium says blue black seems to have been charcoal, named for the blue cast it carries, and that the term was in general use in England by the second half of the seventeenth century [2]. A recipe attributed to the painter Gyles tells readers to burn cuttings of vine as one would ivory black, which makes a fine blue black [2].

Bone black and ivory black are cousins. Coles writes that until the Middle Ages bone black was less widely used than charcoal black, probably because bone is hard to grind to a fine powder, and that bone black sold today often goes under the name ivory black [5]. Jarman, in his own poetic way, describes ivory black as charcoal formed by heating shavings of ivory and bone [12]. The compendium adds a different class, fusain, which is fossil charcoal or, in French, a charcoal crayon made from the spindle tree [2].

sections.title: The black that does not dye
sections.body:
Charcoal is a pigment, not a dye, and that is why black cloth was so hard. Finlay points out that there are no true black dyes, and pigments such as charcoal and soot are not soluble in water, so they do not fix to cloth [3]. Dyers worked around this by dipping cloth in several vats of blue, red and yellow until the result looked black, which was expensive [3].

Cheating was therefore tempting. Pastoureau reports that some dyers who lacked a decent black simply rubbed lampblack or charcoal onto cloth, which gave a handsome uniform color at first but was volatile and impermanent [6]. The fraud was soon found out, and quarrels and lawsuits followed [6]. Logwood, a New World dyewood brought home on Spanish ships, was banned in England in 1581 and permitted again in 1673 [3].

sections.title: Ink, tattoos and eye makeup
sections.body:
Charcoal's cousin soot goes further than painting. Egyptian clerks carried black ink made from soot mixed with gum, and Chinese ink is also mainly soot, from burning pine logs, oil, lacquer resin, or even wine lees [3]. Roman women darkened their eyelashes and the edges of their eyes with ash, various charcoals and antimony powder [10].

Finlay notes that some tattoo traditions made pigment from burned coconut husks, and that European sailors used charcoal soot for the indigo-looking color, because black under pale skin tends to go blue [14]. Here the black is not a surface pigment but a line sunk under the skin, close in spirit to the first drawing on a cave wall.

sections.title: Seeing like charcoal
sections.body:
Charcoal teaches the eye to see value, the dark and light of things. Livingstone points out that people treat charcoal drawings and black-and-white films as unreal, yet in dim light human vision has no color, so everyone sees that way at night [9]. A charcoal drawing is, in that sense, the most natural picture there is.

An ancient writer quoted by Birren noticed that black things heated in a fire turn crimson, and named smoky flame and charcoal under intense heat as examples [8]. Watch glowing charcoal from a barbecue and you will see what he meant: the black goes red when it burns.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of the charcoal swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 400 works, about 1.7 per cent [15]. It plays a shadow role: of those works, the matching color sits in the shadows of 65 per cent and in the mid-tones of 35 per cent, never in the highlights [15]. The match is strongest in the twentieth century, where it appears in 63 of 1,674 paintings, 2.2 times the archive rate, and the 1940s are the peak decade with 6 of 28 [15].

The richest single match is Carl Bloch's *Descent from the Cross* of 1886, where the swatch fills 82 per cent of the image [15]. Fra Angelico's *Madonna of Humility* of 1440 covers 44 per cent, and Odilon Redon's *The Prayer* of 1893 about 42 per cent [15]. Among painters, [[painter:paul-gauguin|Gauguin]] has 8 of 50 works, and by movement Post-Impressionism has 4 of 45 and Impressionism 9 of 140 [15]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so they show screen colors, not pigment tests [15].

origin.first_recorded: as a pigment and drawing material since prehistory; the English color word is undocumented in our books

questions.answer: There are no true black dyes, and charcoal as a pigment will not fix to cloth

openers: The oldest paintings in Europe are drawn in charcoal: the bison of Altamira are outlined in it.
Glowing charcoal turns red, and an ancient writer used that to argue that black mixed with fire gives crimson.
Next time you see a faint grey smudge at the edge of an old painting, think of a baker's oven: that is where Cennini told painters to make their charcoal.

issues: Cave dates: Finlay only (15,000 / 30,000 years); not cross-checked.
The ancient writer on charcoal turning crimson is unnamed in the passage read (Birren ch. 2); hedged.
The statement that painters borrowed the baker's oven is Ball on medieval English painters, distinct from Cennini's recipe.
Percy Coate and the Altamira discovery are single-source (Finlay).
